What the spec step said it changed, its final output:

- **Linux:**
  - Every child process starts with `oom_score_adj` set to 1000, which everything it starts inherits, and containers run with `--oom-score-adj=1000`. That marks them to be ended first.

  - Where systemd is present, run targets and host tasks also run in their own user scope (`systemd-run --user --scope`), so the system's memory handling ends that scope and not Suspense.
- **macOS and Windows:** they give no equivalent control. Each child runs in its own process group or job object, so a child killed for memory takes nothing else with it and Suspense keeps running.
- **Reporting:**
  - A run target killed this way reads "Ran out of memory" instead of a bare exit code.
  - A task or spec build fails saying the machine ran out of memory, naming the program.
  - The debug log records it the same way.

The systemd scope is my addition, and it only helps where systemd is present.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `ApplicationScope` `#memory-pressure` and `#child-processes`, `RunTargetsScope` `#stopping`, and `ContainerEnvironmentScope` `#description`.

content.content:
#### Memory Pressure

When the machine runs out of memory, the operating system ends the program using it rather than Suspense. Every child process the application starts, and everything those start in turn, a run target's build, a task's harness and the commands it runs on the host, piton, git, and each container, is marked as the one to end first, and Suspense itself is never marked so, so a heavy build that uses up memory is what the system ends, never the window holding the user's work.
On Linux, each child process is started with its `oom_score_adj` set to 1000, written to `/proc/self/oom_score_adj` in the child just before it runs its program, so it and all it starts inherit it, and each container is run with `--oom-score-adj=1000`; Suspense keeps its own as it was given, never raising it. Where the system runs systemd, each run target and each task on the host also runs in a transient user scope of its own, as `systemd-run --user --scope` gives, so the system's out-of-memory handling ends that scope and not Suspense's. On macOS and Windows, which give no such control, each child runs in a process group or job object of its own, as a run target already does, so a child ended for its memory takes nothing with it, and Suspense keeps running.
A child ended for running out of memory says so: a run target reads "Ran out of memory" in its error colour, and a task or a spec build fails saying the process was ended because the machine ran out of memory, naming the program, as its exit by SIGKILL with the system recording an out-of-memory kill shows, rather than only its exit status. The debug log records it the same way.

#### Finding Programs

content.text:
When memory runs out, the OS should now end the heavy child process, such as a Rust build, instead of Suspense. All tests pass, including a new one checking that a heavy child starts with an out-of-memory score of 1000 and Suspense keeps its own. I haven't triggered a real out-of-memory kill to watch it happen.

- **Linux:**
  - Run targets, host harness runs and `piton build` set their out-of-memory score to 1000 inside the child just before their program starts, so everything they start, like `rustc` under cargo, inherits it.
  - Every other child started through the logged spawn path is marked right after it starts.
  - Containers run with `--oom-score-adj=1000`, and Suspense never changes its own score.
- **systemd:** where your systemd user session is available, run targets and host harness runs also start in their own user scope via `systemd-run --user --scope`. Suspense checks once that this works; otherwise they start as before.
- **Reporting:** if the system recorded an out-of-memory kill when the child died:
  - a run target reads "Ran out of memory" in red;
  - a task or spec build fails saying the program "was ended because the machine ran out of memory";
  - the debug log records it the same way.
- **Also:** direct `git`/`piton`/`tar`/`cp` calls now go through the same process helper, so they get the right PATH and no console window on Windows too.

Where I departed from the spec:
- **Short-lived commands:** setting the score inside each child before its program starts (what the spec asks for every child) made every spawn much slower, about 77s against 17s in one UI test. So I kept that only for the heavy runs. Short-lived commands like `git` are marked just after they start instead. Those started via `output()` or `status()` aren't marked at all.
- **macOS and Windows:** run targets and host harness runs already get their own process group (and a job object for run targets on Windows). I didn't add one for every other child.
